screens.title: Container and Serverless Security
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore the security surface of two cloud-native paradigms: containers and serverless functions. Containers package applications and share the host kernel, so image hygiene, minimal runtimes, and orchestration controls are essential. Serverless shifts responsibility to code and configuration, making identity, input validation, and secrets handling central to safety. You will learn concrete Dockerfile hardening steps, how to scan and sign images, Kubernetes controls such as Pod Security Standards, Network Policies and RBAC, and serverless practices like least-privilege IAM roles and runtime monitoring. For each area I will show a short example you can apply in CI/CD pipelines and a simple misconception to avoid — for example, believing that containers are VMs and therefore automatically isolate everything. That misconception leads teams to omit host hardening and RBAC restrictions. By the end of this module you will be able to identify attack vectors, apply secure build and deployment practices, and choose runtime monitoring tools to detect threats. Think about one application you manage and where its images and functions are stored — that is where we will begin hardening.

In this lesson

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These four objectives focus your attention on the concrete skills required for container and serverless security. First, you will identify unique attack vectors for containers and functions: know how shared kernels, image supply chains, and event-driven entry points create different risks than classic VMs. Second, you will implement secure practices for building Docker images: using minimal bases, multi-stage builds, removing build tools, and running as a non-root user. Third, you will configure Kubernetes controls such as Pod Security Standards, Network Policies, and RBAC to limit privileges and network reach within clusters. Fourth, you will apply serverless best practices like granting least privilege IAM roles, validating inputs rigorously, and keeping secrets out of code. Each objective pairs conceptual understanding with a concrete task you can perform in a CI/CD pipeline or deployment configuration. For example, after objective two you will be able to rewrite a vulnerable Dockerfile into a hardened multi-stage file and explain why that reduces attack surface. A common misconception is that one control solves everything; instead, success requires layered controls across build, deploy, and runtime. These objectives prepare you to evaluate and operate secure cloud-native workloads.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Continued
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide emphasizes runtime security and operational practices that complete the security lifecycle for cloud-native workloads. You will evaluate tools and strategies for runtime monitoring and protection — for example, using Falco for system call detection or Cilium for networking and eBPF-based observability. Practically, this means integrating runtime detection into your SIEM and configuring alerts for suspicious process behavior, unexpected container privileges, or anomalous network flows. We also stress continuous testing: add image scanning to CI so vulnerabilities are caught before images are deployed, and sign images to ensure integrity. An important misconception to avoid is thinking scanning alone is sufficient; scanning finds known vulnerabilities, while runtime tools detect active exploitation and configuration drift. By combining pre-deployment scanning, signing, Kubernetes admission controls, and runtime monitoring, you build a layered defense. After this objective you should be able to propose a runtime monitoring strategy for a given deployment and justify the combination of tools you selected.

screens.title: Containers vs Serverless — Shared and distinct risks
screens.narratorSegment: Start by distinguishing the two paradigms so you can reason about the right controls. Containers package an application and its dependencies into a portable unit that shares the host kernel. That sharing reduces isolation compared with virtual machines and means that a compromised container can impact host resources unless the host and orchestration layer are hardened. Serverless functions, by contrast, remove server management from your responsibility but make code and configuration the dominant risk surface. For example, a container image with an outdated OS package exposes the running container and, potentially, the host if privilege escalation is possible. A serverless function with an overly broad IAM role can access many cloud resources if compromised, creating a large blast radius. A common misconception is to treat containers like VMs and rely solely on VM-level controls; this overlooks image supply chain and orchestration threats. Concrete example: an application packaged into a Docker image using a full distribution image versus a minimal image — the larger image likely contains more packages with known vulnerabilities that must be scanned and patched. Closing takeaway: map the responsibilities — you secure the image, the orchestration layer, and function policies, while cloud providers manage infrastructure slices; design controls appropriate to who manages what. How would you reassign responsibilities for an app you manage?

keyIdea.title: Comparison insight
keyIdea.text: Containers require image and host hardening; serverless requires strict identity and configuration controls.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Containers vs Serverless
Containers — Typical risks
  • Share host kernel; host compromise risk if container escapes or runs privileged.
  • Image supply chain issues: vulnerable OS packages and dependencies inside images.
  • Misconfigured container runtime or elevated capabilities increase attack surface.
Concrete example
A full distribution base image includes many packages. A single unpatched package can be an attack vector; scanning and minimizing bases reduce risk.
Serverless — Typical risks
  • Permissions and identity are the primary risk: overly broad IAM roles create large blast radii.
  • Input validation mistakes cause injection or unauthorized actions.
  • Secrets exposed in code or environment variables can be exfiltrated.
Concrete example
A function granted broad S3 permissions can read unrelated buckets; least-privilege policies limit scope and damage if the function is compromised.
Key Takeaway

Match controls to architecture: reduce image size and enforce host protections for containers; enforce identity and input controls for serverless.

screens.title: Container image security and supply chain
screens.narratorSegment: A secure container starts with a secure image. Image hygiene means choosing minimal base images, removing build tools, using multi-stage builds, scanning for known vulnerabilities, and signing images so consumers can verify integrity. Minimal bases reduce the number of packages you must patch and scan, lowering the chance a vulnerable library is present. Multi-stage builds allow you to use build-time compilers and then omit them from the final runtime image. Scanning tools integrated into CI detect known CVEs in OS packages and language dependencies; these tools do not fix all problems but flag issues early so you can patch or replace packages. Signing images with tools like Cosign or Notary adds provenance so the deploy pipeline can reject unsigned images. A concrete example is replacing a large distribution image with a slim or scratch-based image and moving compilation into a builder stage. A common misconception is to trust 'latest' tags; in practice 'latest' is mutable and creates reproducibility and supply-chain risk. The takeaway: treat images as code artifacts — version them, scan them, and enforce signature checks before deployment. Which image in your pipeline would you sign first?

keyIdea.title: Image hygiene
keyIdea.text: Use minimal bases, multi-stage builds, scanning, and signing to control the supply chain and reduce vulnerabilities.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Image Security
Image hygiene checklist
  • Choose minimal base images and avoid mutable 'latest' tags.
  • Use multi-stage builds to remove build-time dependencies from final images.
  • Run containers as non-root users and remove compilers and debuggers.
  • Scan images in CI and sign images for provenance checks at deployment.
Common Mistake
Running containers as root and using large base images increases exploitability and potential host impact.
Example
# Vulnerable example
FROM ubuntu:latest
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl python3-pip
COPY . /app
WORKDIR /app
RUN pip3 install -r requirements.txt
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["python3","app.py"]

# More secure: multi-stage and non-root
# Stage 1: Build
FROM python:3.9-slim-buster as builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Stage 2: Final image
FROM python:3.9-slim-buster
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /usr/local/lib/python3.9/site-packages /usr/local/lib/python3.9/site-packages
COPY . .
RUN adduser --system --no-create-home appuser
USER appuser
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["python3","app.py"]
Key Takeaway

Images are supply chain artifacts: minimize, scan, and sign them to protect deployments and ensure integrity.

screens.title: Hardening a Dockerfile — step-by-step demo
screens.narratorSegment: In this walkthrough we move from a basic, vulnerable Dockerfile to a hardened multi-stage example that follows best practices. The vulnerable file often uses a full language image without cleaning build tools, runs as root, and uses mutable tags. We will apply four concrete changes: choose a smaller base where possible, separate build-time dependencies into a builder stage, remove build tools from the runtime image, and create and switch to a non-root user. For example, a simple vulnerable file uses 'python:3.9' and runs package installs in the final image. Rewriting it into a builder stage performs installs and compiles dependencies, then copies only the resulting site-packages into a slim runtime image. Running as a non-root user reduces privileges inside the container and mitigates the impact of a process compromise. A misconception is believing that adding a non-root user alone is enough; it must be combined with removing capabilities and enforcing read-only filesystems where possible. After this demo you should be able to edit a Dockerfile to implement multi-stage builds and identify remaining risks to address during image scanning and runtime hardening. Which change would you prioritize in your pipeline?

keyIdea.title: Hardening steps
keyIdea.text: Use builder stages, minimal runtime images, non-root users, and remove build tools to shrink attack surface before scanning and signing.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Dockerfile Hardening
Transformations applied
  1. Use multi-stage build to separate build-time dependencies from runtime.
  2. Select minimal runtime images and avoid mutable tags.
  3. Create and switch to a non-root user in the final image.
  4. Remove compilers, set read-only filesystem where possible, and minimize installed packages.
Misconception
Adding a non-root user alone does not prevent privilege escalation if capabilities are granted or the host is misconfigured; combine controls.
Code Walkthrough
# Stage 1: Builder
FROM python:3.9-slim-buster as builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Stage 2: Final image
FROM python:3.9-slim-buster
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /usr/local/lib/python3.9/site-packages /usr/local/lib/python3.9/site-packages
COPY . .
# Create non-root user and switch
RUN adduser --system --no-create-home appuser
USER appuser
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["python3","app.py"]
Key Takeaway

Refactor Dockerfiles into builder and runtime stages, and enforce non-root execution plus minimal packages before scanning and signing.

screens.title: Image scanning and signing in CI/CD
screens.narratorSegment: Integrating image scanning and signing into CI/CD pipelines turns manual checks into enforceable gates. The process begins on code commit: build the image in a builder agent, run a scanner such as Trivy or Clair to check OS packages and language dependencies for known CVEs, and fail the build if critical vulnerabilities are found. Next, add metadata and sign the image with a tool like Cosign so downstream stages can verify provenance. Enforce signature verification in deployment by requiring only signed images in admission controllers or pipeline policies. A practical example: when a pull request triggers a pipeline, a scan job runs and posts results; if the scan passes a rule set, an image signing job runs and the pipeline publishes the signed artifact to the registry. A misconception is to run scans only ad-hoc; without CI enforcement, images with high-severity findings may be deployed. The final step is to ensure alerts feed into ticketing or security triage so developers fix discovered issues. The takeaway: automation ensures scanning and signing are repeatable, enforceable, and observable across teams. Image scanning and signing in CI/CD means automate scanning and signing in pipelines, and require signed images for deployment to ensure integrity and prevent vulnerable builds reaching production.. In practical terms, automating detection and enforcing image provenance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: CI/CD enforcement
keyIdea.text: Automate scanning and signing in pipelines, and require signed images for deployment to ensure integrity and prevent vulnerable builds reaching production.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Scanning & Signing
Pipeline steps
  1. Build image in isolated builder agent.
  2. Run image scanner (Trivy, Clair) and evaluate results against policy.
  3. If pass, sign image (Cosign, Notary) and push to registry.
  4. Enforce signature verification on deploy and at admission time.
Automation benefits
  • Consistent checks and no manual bypasses.
  • Faster feedback to developers and earlier remediation.
  • Provenance for auditing and rollback decisions.
Concrete scenario
A PR triggers CI: a scan job runs and a signing job only runs if the scan passes defined severity thresholds. Signed images are pushed to the registry and admission controllers reject unsigned images at deploy time.
Misconception: scanning once is enough. In reality, images should be rescanned periodically and before production promotion.
Key Takeaway

Put scans and signatures into CI gates. Enforcement must be automated to prevent vulnerable or unsigned images from reaching production.

screens.title: Kubernetes security pillars
screens.narratorSegment: Kubernetes adds an orchestration layer that must be managed securely. The main pillars are Pod Security Standards, Role-Based Access Control, Network Policies, secrets management, and logging/monitoring. Pod Security Standards define profiles like Restricted, Baseline, and Privileged to control capabilities and system calls; the Restricted profile enforces runAsNonRoot, disallows privilege escalation, drops capabilities, and encourages read-only root filesystems. RBAC limits what principals — users, groups, and service accounts — can do within the cluster; grant least privilege to service accounts tied to workloads. Network Policies control pod-to-pod and pod-to-external traffic; without them, pods can talk to anything by default. Secrets should be stored with an external manager when possible; Kubernetes Secrets are base64-encoded and require additional protections such as encryption at rest and limited RBAC access. Finally, logging and monitoring collect telemetry from pods and nodes and feed SIEM for threat detection and incident response. A common misconception is that enabling one feature, like RBAC, eliminates network-level threats — in practice you need all pillars working together. Consider a deployment using Restricted PSS, narrow RBAC, deny-by-default Network Policies and external secret storage as a balanced architecture for most production workloads.

keyIdea.title: Kubernetes pillars
keyIdea.text: Apply Pod Security Standards, fine-grained RBAC, network segmentation, secrets best practices, and centralized logging to secure clusters.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Kubernetes Security
Security pillars
Pod Security Standards (Restricted, Baseline, Privileged)
Role-Based Access Control (least privilege for users and service accounts)
Network Policies (deny-by-default segmentation)
Secrets & external secret managers
Example enforcement
Combine Restricted PSS for workload admission, RBAC to limit API actions, and deny-all Network Policies that only allow required flows.
Operational items
  • Enable audit logging and forward to SIEM.
  • Rotate and audit service-account permissions.
  • Integrate runtime tools like Falco for detection of suspicious syscalls.
Key Takeaway

No single control suffices. Use PSS, RBAC, Network Policies, secrets management, and logging together to reduce risk in Kubernetes clusters.

screens.title: Pod Security Standards & securityContext example
screens.narratorSegment: Pod Security Standards and the securityContext fields provide concrete, enforceable controls for pods. The Restricted profile is most secure and enforces settings like runAsNonRoot, runAsUser, disallowing privilege escalation, dropping capabilities, and read-only root filesystems where appropriate. A practical YAML snippet shows how to set these fields at the pod or container level so they are applied consistently. For example, runAsUser set to a non-zero UID ensures containers do not run as root, and allowPrivilegeEscalation set to false prevents processes from gaining additional privileges. Dropping ALL capabilities removes Linux capabilities that are often unnecessary. A common misconception is configuring these only at the container level; configuring at the Pod level as well provides consistent defaults for all containers in the pod. Concrete example: adding securityContext with runAsNonRoot true and readOnlyRootFilesystem true reduces attack vectors where an attacker could modify files in the container. The takeaway: use PSS profiles and explicit securityContext fields as admission checks to prevent unsafe pods from running. Pod Security Standards & securityContext example means use pod security standards and securitycontext fields to enforce non-root execution, drop capabilities, and disallow privilege escalation.. In practical terms, enforce runasnonroot, drop capabilities, and prevent privilege escalation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pod-level controls
keyIdea.text: Use Pod Security Standards and securityContext fields to enforce non-root execution, drop capabilities, and disallow privilege escalation.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › PSS & securityContext
Pod security context example
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-app
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: my-app
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 1000
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault
      containers:
      - name: my-container
        image: my-secure-image:latest
        securityContext:
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          capabilities:
            drop:
            - ALL
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
Applying these fields prevents privilege escalation, removes unnecessary capabilities, and reduces the writable surface inside a container.
Checklist
  • Set runAsNonRoot and runAsUser for deterministic UIDs.
  • Set allowPrivilegeEscalation to false.
  • Drop ALL capabilities unless explicitly required.

screens.title: Network Policies and RBAC
screens.narratorSegment: Two controls work together to narrow an attacker’s options inside a cluster: Network Policies for traffic segmentation and RBAC for A P I-level permissions. By default Kubernetes permits all pod-to-pod traffic; Network Policies change that to an allowlist model where only specified ingress and egress flows are permitted. For example, a deny-all ingress + explicit egress rules force services to declare their communication needs and block lateral movement. RBAC restricts what users and service accounts can do in the A P I, preventing a compromised pod from creating or deleting cluster resources unless those permissions are explicitly granted. A concrete YAML example is a NetworkPolicy with empty ingress and egress arrays to deny all traffic unless allowed. A common misconception is that Network Policies protect against compromised containers accessing node-level services — they operate at the pod network layer and should be combined with host-level firewalls and cluster hardening. The practical takeaway: implement deny-by-default Network Policies and least-privilege RBAC for service accounts to sharply reduce the potential for lateral movement and misuse of the Kubernetes A P I. In practical terms, limiting traffic and api permissions to reduce blast radius. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Network Policies & RBAC
Deny-by-default NetworkPolicy
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-all-ingress
  namespace: default
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
  ingress: []
  egress: []
This policy denies all ingress and egress unless other policies explicitly allow traffic, forcing teams to declare required flows.
RBAC guidance
  • Assign least-privilege roles to service accounts used by workloads.
  • Audit cluster roles and bindings for unexpected broad permissions.
  • Rotate credentials and avoid reusing high-privilege service accounts for many apps.
Misconception

Network Policies limit pod network flows but are not a substitute for host hardening or admission controls. Combine controls for defense-in-depth.

screens.title: Serverless security fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: Serverless removes server management but concentrates security responsibilities in identity, code, and configuration. The most important control is Identity and Access Management: grant each function the least privilege it needs, avoid wildcard permissions, and use resource-based policies to limit which functions can access which resources. Input validation is the second major area: functions process events and external requests, so every input must be validated and sanitized to prevent injection and unexpected behavior. Secrets must never be hardcoded; use dedicated secret managers and retrieve secrets at runtime with appropriate permissions. If functions are exposed via an A P I Gateway, enforce authentication and authorization there, apply rate limiting, and integrate with a web application firewall where appropriate. A common misconception is that small, ephemeral functions are low-risk; function compromise with broad IAM rights can have severe consequences. Concrete example: give a Lambda function s3:GetObject only for its specific input bucket rather than s3:* on all buckets. The takeaway: treat functions as applications — design narrow roles, sanitize input, and protect exposed endpoints through A P I Gateway controls. Serverless security fundamentals means apply least privilege iam, rigorous input validation, secrets management, and api gateway protections to secure functions.. In practical terms, iam, input validation, secrets, and api gateway protections. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Serverless Fundamentals
IAM least-privilege example
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "logs:CreateLogGroup",
        "logs:CreateLogStream",
        "logs:PutLogEvents"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:logs:*:*:*"
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "s3:GetObject"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-secure-bucket/input/*"
    }
  ]
}
This policy grants only logging and a specific GetObject permission on a single input bucket, minimizing blast radius.
Serverless checklist
  • Assign dedicated IAM roles per function with minimal permissions.
  • Validate and sanitize all inputs from event sources and APIs.
  • Store secrets in an external manager and retrieve at runtime with strict access controls.
  • Protect exposed functions with API Gateway authentication and rate limiting.
Misconception

Serverless is not automatically secure because infrastructure is managed. The code, roles, and configuration you create determine risk and blast radius.

screens.title: Runtime protection and monitoring
screens.narratorSegment: Pre-deployment checks reduce risk, but runtime monitoring detects active threats and configuration drift. Tools such as Falco observe system calls and identify suspicious behavior inside containers; Cilium and eBPF-based tools provide network-level observability and policy enforcement. For serverless functions, detailed logging and anomaly detection in CloudWatch or Azure Monitor help identify unusual invocation patterns or error spikes. The runtime strategy should include detection, alerting, and playbooks for triage and containment. For example, a Falco rule can alert when a container spawns a shell or modifies critical binaries — actions often associated with exploitation. Integrate alerts into your SIEM and provide context like image ID, pod name, and associated service account to speed investigation. A common misconception is that runtime tools replace pre-deploy scanning; they complement it by catching behavior that scanning cannot predict. Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Runtime Security
Detection & response patterns
  • Instrument hosts and pods with runtime detectors (Falco) to watch for suspicious syscalls and process activity.
  • Use network observability tools (Cilium, eBPF) to detect anomalous flows and enforce segmentation.
  • Forward logs and alerts to SIEM and tie them to identity and image metadata for context.
  • Create playbooks for containment, image quarantine, and credential rotation after detection.
Concrete detection rule
A Falco rule might alert on unexpected shells spawned by a web process or write to /etc, signaling potential compromise. Correlate with image and service account to decide containment steps.
Operational tip
Ensure alerts include image digest, pod name, and service account so responders can act quickly and revoke permissions if needed.
Key Takeaway

Runtime monitoring detects active threats and should be integrated with SIEM and runbooks to enable fast containment and recovery.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore the security surface of two cloud-native paradigms: containers and serverless functions. Containers package applications and share the host kernel, so image hygiene, minimal runtimes, and orchestration controls are essential. Serverless shifts responsibility to code and configuration, making identity, input validation, and secrets handling central to safety. You will learn concrete Dockerfile hardening steps, how to scan and sign images, Kubernetes controls such as Pod Security Standards, Network Policies and RBAC, and serverless practices like least-privilege IAM roles and runtime monitoring. For each area I will show a short example you can apply in CI/CD pipelines and a simple misconception to avoid — for example, believing that containers are VMs and therefore automatically isolate everything. That misconception leads teams to omit host hardening and RBAC restrictions. By the end of this module you will be able to identify attack vectors, apply secure build and deployment practices, and choose runtime monitoring tools to detect threats. Think about one application you manage and where its images and functions are stored — that is where we will begin hardening.

These four objectives focus your attention on the concrete skills required for container and serverless security. First, you will identify unique attack vectors for containers and functions: know how shared kernels, image supply chains, and event-driven entry points create different risks than classic VMs. Second, you will implement secure practices for building Docker images: using minimal bases, multi-stage builds, removing build tools, and running as a non-root user. Third, you will configure Kubernetes controls such as Pod Security Standards, Network Policies, and RBAC to limit privileges and network reach within clusters. Fourth, you will apply serverless best practices like granting least privilege IAM roles, validating inputs rigorously, and keeping secrets out of code. Each objective pairs conceptual understanding with a concrete task you can perform in a CI/CD pipeline or deployment configuration. For example, after objective two you will be able to rewrite a vulnerable Dockerfile into a hardened multi-stage file and explain why that reduces attack surface. A common misconception is that one control solves everything; instead, success requires layered controls across build, deploy, and runtime. These objectives prepare you to evaluate and operate secure cloud-native workloads.

This second objectives slide emphasizes runtime security and operational practices that complete the security lifecycle for cloud-native workloads. You will evaluate tools and strategies for runtime monitoring and protection — for example, using Falco for system call detection or Cilium for networking and eBPF-based observability. Practically, this means integrating runtime detection into your SIEM and configuring alerts for suspicious process behavior, unexpected container privileges, or anomalous network flows. We also stress continuous testing: add image scanning to CI so vulnerabilities are caught before images are deployed, and sign images to ensure integrity. An important misconception to avoid is thinking scanning alone is sufficient; scanning finds known vulnerabilities, while runtime tools detect active exploitation and configuration drift. By combining pre-deployment scanning, signing, Kubernetes admission controls, and runtime monitoring, you build a layered defense. After this objective you should be able to propose a runtime monitoring strategy for a given deployment and justify the combination of tools you selected.

Start by distinguishing the two paradigms so you can reason about the right controls. Containers package an application and its dependencies into a portable unit that shares the host kernel. That sharing reduces isolation compared with virtual machines and means that a compromised container can impact host resources unless the host and orchestration layer are hardened. Serverless functions, by contrast, remove server management from your responsibility but make code and configuration the dominant risk surface. For example, a container image with an outdated OS package exposes the running container and, potentially, the host if privilege escalation is possible. A serverless function with an overly broad IAM role can access many cloud resources if compromised, creating a large blast radius. A common misconception is to treat containers like VMs and rely solely on VM-level controls; this overlooks image supply chain and orchestration threats. Concrete example: an application packaged into a Docker image using a full distribution image versus a minimal image — the larger image likely contains more packages with known vulnerabilities that must be scanned and patched. Closing takeaway: map the responsibilities — you secure the image, the orchestration layer, and function policies, while cloud providers manage infrastructure slices; design controls appropriate to who manages what. How would you reassign responsibilities for an app you manage?

A secure container starts with a secure image. Image hygiene means choosing minimal base images, removing build tools, using multi-stage builds, scanning for known vulnerabilities, and signing images so consumers can verify integrity. Minimal bases reduce the number of packages you must patch and scan, lowering the chance a vulnerable library is present. Multi-stage builds allow you to use build-time compilers and then omit them from the final runtime image. Scanning tools integrated into CI detect known CVEs in OS packages and language dependencies; these tools do not fix all problems but flag issues early so you can patch or replace packages. Signing images with tools like Cosign or Notary adds provenance so the deploy pipeline can reject unsigned images. A concrete example is replacing a large distribution image with a slim or scratch-based image and moving compilation into a builder stage. A common misconception is to trust 'latest' tags; in practice 'latest' is mutable and creates reproducibility and supply-chain risk. The takeaway: treat images as code artifacts — version them, scan them, and enforce signature checks before deployment. Which image in your pipeline would you sign first?

In this walkthrough we move from a basic, vulnerable Dockerfile to a hardened multi-stage example that follows best practices. The vulnerable file often uses a full language image without cleaning build tools, runs as root, and uses mutable tags. We will apply four concrete changes: choose a smaller base where possible, separate build-time dependencies into a builder stage, remove build tools from the runtime image, and create and switch to a non-root user. For example, a simple vulnerable file uses 'python:3.9' and runs package installs in the final image. Rewriting it into a builder stage performs installs and compiles dependencies, then copies only the resulting site-packages into a slim runtime image. Running as a non-root user reduces privileges inside the container and mitigates the impact of a process compromise. A misconception is believing that adding a non-root user alone is enough; it must be combined with removing capabilities and enforcing read-only filesystems where possible. After this demo you should be able to edit a Dockerfile to implement multi-stage builds and identify remaining risks to address during image scanning and runtime hardening. Which change would you prioritize in your pipeline?

Integrating image scanning and signing into CI/CD pipelines turns manual checks into enforceable gates. The process begins on code commit: build the image in a builder agent, run a scanner such as Trivy or Clair to check OS packages and language dependencies for known CVEs, and fail the build if critical vulnerabilities are found. Next, add metadata and sign the image with a tool like Cosign so downstream stages can verify provenance. Enforce signature verification in deployment by requiring only signed images in admission controllers or pipeline policies. A practical example: when a pull request triggers a pipeline, a scan job runs and posts results; if the scan passes a rule set, an image signing job runs and the pipeline publishes the signed artifact to the registry. A misconception is to run scans only ad-hoc; without CI enforcement, images with high-severity findings may be deployed. The final step is to ensure alerts feed into ticketing or security triage so developers fix discovered issues. The takeaway: automation ensures scanning and signing are repeatable, enforceable, and observable across teams. Image scanning and signing in CI/CD means automate scanning and signing in pipelines, and require signed images for deployment to ensure integrity and prevent vulnerable builds reaching production.. In practical terms, automating detection and enforcing image provenance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Kubernetes adds an orchestration layer that must be managed securely. The main pillars are Pod Security Standards, Role-Based Access Control, Network Policies, secrets management, and logging/monitoring. Pod Security Standards define profiles like Restricted, Baseline, and Privileged to control capabilities and system calls; the Restricted profile enforces runAsNonRoot, disallows privilege escalation, drops capabilities, and encourages read-only root filesystems. RBAC limits what principals — users, groups, and service accounts — can do within the cluster; grant least privilege to service accounts tied to workloads. Network Policies control pod-to-pod and pod-to-external traffic; without them, pods can talk to anything by default.
